newsitem.title: USA: Mrs. Clinton says loans can change lives of poor.
newsitem.headline: Mrs. Clinton says loans can change lives of poor.

text.p: First lady Hillary Rodham Clinton said Monday that small loans -- some as low as $125 -- could change the lives of poor people around the globe and urged an expansion of small lines of credit to them.

Mrs. Clinton told an international conference that many low-income people were excellent credit risks but many banks were still reluctant to give them loans for small businesses or other projects that could lift them from poverty.

The first lady addressed the "Microcredit Summit" of 2,500 representatives from 115 countries pledged to expand the availability of credit to 100 million of the world's poorest families by the year 2005.

"I think if more banks understood the tenacity, the commitment, the entrepreneurial spirit of people like these who were given a chance to help themselves, we would go a long way in not only extending credit, but in eliminating many of the unfortunate stereotypes about people who are poor," Mrs. Clinton said.
Many poor people who ask for a loan to start or extend a small business work "as hard as they know how," she said.

"Yet too often those of us in positions of influence or authority or power dismiss them. We seem to have a belief that if they are poor they are meant to be poor and will always remain poor," she said.
The audience of 2,500 included representatives of public, private and non-profit organisations in the microcredit movement to help people who are outside the conventional banking system.

The movement traces its roots to the 1970s when a Bangladeshi economist, Muhammed Yunus, started the Grameen Bank for the poor. In many countries, typical uses of loans are for buying cattle, or products for agriculture, and the loans are as small as a few dollars.

In the United States, the loans may be larger -- Mrs Clinton mentioned some from the Small Business Association that range from $125 to $25,000 -- and typically go for businesses with five or fewer employees.

World Bank Vice President Ismail Serageldin told reporters that some 7,000 grassoroots institutions currently are reaching out with some $8 billion of loans to over 13 million low-income customers, many of them women.

But the conference organisers estimate that up to $21.6 billion in grants, low interest loans, and commercial loans could be needed to achieve their goal of expanding credit to 100 million families by 2,005.

The organisers insist that the conference itself is not intended as a fund-raiser. But United Nations Development Programme Administrator James Speth is expected to announce Tuesday the creation of a new $41 million programme to improve access to small loans in developing countries.

Last week President Clinton announced he would request $1 billion over five years to support development of a "microenterprise development program" to increase access to credit for women, low-income people and minorities.
